front: What Protocol Data Unit (PDU) corresponds to Layer 2 of the OSI model?
back: Data Link Layer -> Frames (contains source and destination MAC addresses)

front: What Protocol Data Unit (PDU) corresponds to Layer 3 of the OSI model?
back: Network Layer -> Packets (contains source and destination IP addresses)

front: What Protocol Data Unit (PDU) corresponds to Layer 4 of the OSI model?
back: Transport Layer -> Segments (for TCP) or Datagrams (for UDP)

front: What Protocol Data Unit (PDU) corresponds to Layer 1 of the OSI model?
back: Physical Layer -> Bits (electrical signals, light pulses, radio waves)

front: Map the 4 layers of the TCP/IP (DoD) model to the 7-layer OSI model.
back:
1. Application (OSI Layers 7, 6, 5: App, Pres, Sess)
2. Transport / Host-to-Host (OSI Layer 4)
3. Internet (OSI Layer 3)
4. Network Access / Link (OSI Layers 2 & 1)

front: What ports are used by FTP and what are their specific functions?
back: TCP 20 (FTP Data Transfer) and TCP 21 (FTP Control / Command Channel)

front: What port and transport protocol does SSH (Secure Shell) use?
back: TCP port 22 (provides encrypted remote CLI access and SFTP)

front: What port does Telnet use and why is it considered insecure?
back: TCP port 23. It transmits all traffic including credentials in plaintext with no encryption.

front: What port is used for unencrypted SMTP relay, and what port is standard for secure SMTP client submission?
back: TCP 25 (standard relay / unencrypted), TCP 587 (Submission with STARTTLS / TLS)

front: What port does DNS use and when does it use UDP vs TCP?
back: Port 53. Uses UDP 53 for standard name queries; uses TCP 53 for zone transfers (AXFR) and responses exceeding 512 bytes.

front: What ports are used by DHCP and which is server vs client?
back: UDP 67 (DHCP Server listening) and UDP 68 (DHCP Client listening)

front: What port and transport protocol does TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) use?
back: UDP port 69 (connectionless, no authentication, commonly used for PXE boot & router configs)

front: What port is used by HTTP and what port is used by HTTPS?
back: TCP 80 for plaintext HTTP; TCP 443 for HTTPS (HTTP over TLS/SSL)

front: What are the default ports for POP3 (cleartext) and POP3S (secure)?
back: TCP 110 for POP3; TCP 995 for POP3S (SSL/TLS encrypted)

front: What port and transport protocol does NTP (Network Time Protocol) use?
back: UDP port 123 (used to synchronize system clocks over packet-switched networks)

front: What are the default ports for IMAP (cleartext) and IMAPS (secure)?
back: TCP 143 for IMAP; TCP 993 for IMAPS (SSL/TLS encrypted)

front: What ports are used by SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) queries and SNMP traps?
back: UDP 161 for SNMP queries/polls (manager to agent); UDP 162 for SNMP Traps/Informs (agent notifications to manager)

front: What ports are used by LDAP and LDAPS?
back: TCP 389 for unencrypted LDAP; TCP 636 for LDAPS (LDAP over SSL/TLS)

front: What port does SMB (Server Message Block) use for direct TCP/IP file sharing?
back: TCP port 445 (direct host SMB without NetBIOS)

front: What port and transport protocol does Syslog typically use for logging?
back: UDP port 514 (default cleartext event logging; TCP 6514 used for TLS Syslog)

front: What port does Microsoft RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) operate on?
back: TCP port 3389 (UDP 3389 optionally used for enhanced performance)

front: What are the three RFC 1918 private IPv4 address ranges?
What IPv4 address range is reserved for APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing / Link-Local)?
back: 169.254.0.0/16 (169.254.0.1 to 169.254.255.254). Assigned automatically when DHCP fails.

front: What are the default subnet masks and first-octet ranges for Class A, B, and C IPv4 addresses?
back:
Class A: 1-126 (Default Mask: 255.0.0.0 /8)
Class B: 128-191 (Default Mask: 255.255.0.0 /16)
Class C: 192-223 (Default Mask: 255.255.255.0 /24)
(127.0.0.0/8 is reserved for loopback)

front: How many total and usable IP addresses exist in a /28 subnet?
back:
Total: 2^(32-28) = 2^4 = 16 addresses.
Usable: 16 - 2 = 14 usable host IPs (subnet mask: 255.255.255.240).

front: What is the subnet mask and usable host count for a point-to-point /30 subnet?
back: Subnet Mask: 255.255.255.252. Total: 4 addresses. Usable: 2 host IPs (one for each router interface).

front: Identify the IPv6 prefix and purpose of Link-Local addresses.
back: Prefix: fe80::/10 (typically fe80:: through febf::). Non-routable beyond local link, auto-generated on every IPv6 interface.

front: Identify the IPv6 prefix and purpose of Global Unicast addresses (GUA).
back: Prefix: 2000::/3 (currently 2000:: through 3fff::). Publicly routable across the global internet, equivalent to public IPv4.

front: Identify the IPv6 Unique Local Address (ULA) prefix and its IPv4 equivalent.
back: Prefix: fc00::/7 (fd00::/8 commonly used). Private, non-routable on the global internet, equivalent to RFC 1918 private IPv4.

front: What is the IPv6 loopback address and unspecified address?
back:
Loopback: ::1/128 (equivalent to 127.0.0.1 in IPv4).
Unspecified: ::/128 (equivalent to 0.0.0.0 in IPv4).

front: What are the maximum transmission speed, bandwidth, and distance for Cat 5e cabling?
back:
Speed: 1 Gbps (1000BASE-T)
Bandwidth: 100 MHz
Max Distance: 100 meters (328 feet)

front: What are the speed and distance limits of Cat 6 cabling at 1 Gbps vs 10 Gbps?
back: 1 Gbps up to 100 meters. 10 Gbps (10GBASE-T) up to 55 meters in standard environments (37m in high crosstalk). Bandwidth: 250 MHz.

front: What are the speed, bandwidth, and distance specifications for Cat 6a cabling?
back:
Speed: 10 Gbps (10GBASE-T)
Bandwidth: 500 MHz
Max Distance: 100 meters (full distance without 55m attenuation penalty)

front: What are the speed, bandwidth, and distance specs of Cat 8 cabling?
back:
Speed: 25 Gbps to 40 Gbps (40GBASE-T)
Bandwidth: 2000 MHz (2 GHz)
Max Distance: 30 meters (designed for data center switch-to-server connections)

front: Compare Single-Mode Fiber (SMF) vs Multi-Mode Fiber (MMF) in core size, light source, and distance.
back:
SMF: Small core (~9 microns), Laser light source, 1310/1550 nm, distances up to tens of km.
MMF: Larger core (50 or 62.5 microns), LED or VCSEL light source, 850/1300 nm, distances up to 300-500 meters (limited by modal dispersion).

front: Identify common fiber connector types: LC, SC, ST, and MPO.
back:
LC (Lucent/Little Connector): Small form-factor with push-pull tab.
SC (Subscriber Connector): Square snap-in push-pull.
ST (Straight Tip): Round bayonet twist-lock.
MPO/MTP: High-density multi-fiber ribbon connector (12-24 fibers).

front: What frequency bands and maximum theoretical throughput does Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) provide?
back:
Bands: 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz (Wi-Fi 6E adds 6 GHz).
Max Throughput: ~9.6 Gbps.
Key Tech: OFDMA, MU-MIMO (up to 8 streams), Target Wake Time (TWT), 1024-QAM.

front: What frequency bands and maximum throughput does Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) introduce?
back:
Bands: 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 6 GHz simultaneously (Multi-Link Operation / MLO).
Max Throughput: Up to 46 Gbps.
Channel Width: Up to 320 MHz; 4096-QAM modulation.

front: What IEEE standard defines VLAN tagging on Ethernet frames, and how many tag bytes are added?
back: IEEE 802.1Q. It inserts a 4-byte (32-bit) tag into the Ethernet frame containing a 12-bit VLAN ID (allowing up to 4094 VLANs).

front: What is the purpose of Spanning Tree Protocol (STP), and what are IEEE 802.1D vs 802.1w?
back: Prevents Layer 2 broadcast storms and bridge loops. IEEE 802.1D is traditional STP (30-50 sec convergence); IEEE 802.1w is Rapid STP / RSTP (converges within milliseconds to seconds).

front: Differentiate Distance-Vector vs Link-State routing protocols with examples.
back:
Distance-Vector: Shares routing table copies with immediate neighbors based on hop count or vector (e.g., RIPv2). Slower convergence.
Link-State: Every router floods link status (LSA) to build a complete topology map via Dijkstra's SPF algorithm (e.g., OSPF, IS-IS). Fast convergence.

front: What type of routing protocol is BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) and what is its primary use?
back: Path-Vector Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP). Used to exchange routing and reachability information between different Autonomous Systems (AS) across the Internet backbone using TCP port 179.

front: What is the standard Ethernet MTU and what is a Jumbo Frame?
back:
Standard Ethernet MTU: 1500 bytes (payload size).
Jumbo Frame: Typically 9000 bytes. Requires end-to-end switch and NIC support to avoid fragmentation and reduce CPU overhead on high-speed SAN/LANs.

front: What is First Hop Redundancy Protocol (FHRP) and name three common FHRP implementations.
back: FHRP provides a default gateway failover mechanism using a shared virtual IP/MAC. Implementations: HSRP (Cisco proprietary/standardized), VRRP (open standard RFC 5798), and GLBP (Cisco load balancing).

front: Compare RADIUS vs TACACS+ in transport protocol, encryption scope, and AAA separation.
back:
RADIUS: UDP (1812/1813 or 1645/1646). Only encrypts the password. Combines Authentication & Authorization.
TACACS+: TCP port 49. Encrypts the entire packet payload. Completely separates Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting.

front: What is IEEE 802.1X and what are its three fundamental entities?
back: Port-based Network Access Control (PNAC). 1. Supplicant (client device wanting access), 2. Authenticator (switch or WAP enforcing access), 3. Authentication Server (RADIUS/EAP server validating credentials).

front: Differentiate IPsec AH (Authentication Header) vs ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload).
back:
AH (Protocol 51): Provides data integrity and authentication, but NO encryption (plaintext payload). Incompatible with NAT.
ESP (Protocol 50): Provides confidentiality (encryption), integrity, and authentication. Can traverse NAT when encapsulated in UDP 4500 (NAT-T).

front: What key cryptographic cipher and handshake protocol distinguish WPA3 from WPA2?
back: WPA3 uses SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) Dragonfly handshake instead of the vulnerable 4-way PSK handshake, preventing offline dictionary attacks and providing forward secrecy. Uses 128-bit or 192-bit GCMP encryption.

front: What is ARP Poisoning / Spoofing and how does Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) mitigate it?
back: An attacker sends gratuitous ARP messages associating their MAC address with the default gateway's IP to execute Man-in-the-Middle (MitM). DAI on switches inspects ARP packets against the DHCP snooping binding database to drop fraudulent ARP responses.

front: What is the difference between a TDR (Time-Domain Reflectometer) and an OTDR (Optical TDR)?
back:
TDR sends electrical pulses down copper twisted-pair cables to locate shorts, opens, and impedance mismatches with distance metrics.
OTDR injects light pulses down optical fiber cables to measure light backscatter and locate fiber breaks, macrobends, and splice losses.

front: What tool combination is used to trace an unlabeled cable from a wall jack to a patch panel?
back: Toner and Probe (Tone Generator / Inductive Amplifier). The generator sends an audible RF tone through the copper pair, and the inductive probe detects the tone when brought near the correct wire.

front: How does `traceroute` (Unix/Linux) differ from `tracert` (Windows) in probe packet type?
back:
Windows `tracert` uses ICMP Echo Request packets with incrementing TTLs.
Linux/macOS `traceroute` defaults to UDP datagrams with high port numbers (33434+) with incrementing TTLs (can optionally use ICMP with `-I`).

front: What command displays active TCP/UDP connections, listening ports, and ethernet statistics on Windows and Linux?
back:
Windows: `netstat -ano` (shows listening ports, protocol, PID).
Linux: `ss -tulpn` (modern socket statistics) or `netstat -tulpn`.

front: List the 7 steps of the CompTIA Network Troubleshooting Methodology in order.
back:
1. Identify the problem (gather info, question users, duplicate problem, determine symptoms)
2. Establish a theory of probable cause (question the obvious, OSI layer approach)
3. Test the theory to determine cause
4. Establish a plan of action and identify potential effects
5. Implement the solution or escalate as necessary
6. Verify full system functionality and implement preventive measures
7. Document findings, actions, and outcomes

front: In a Wireshark packet capture, what TCP flag sequence indicates a normal 3-way handshake?
back:
Packet 1: SYN (Client to Server, sequence number x)
Packet 2: SYN-ACK (Server to Client, ack x+1, sequence number y)
Packet 3: ACK (Client to Server, ack y+1)

front: What port and protocol does Kerberos use, and what is its operational function in Active Directory?
back: TCP/UDP port 88. Enterprise authentication based on symmetric key cryptography and Key Distribution Center (KDC) ticket granting (TGT/TGS), serving as default Active Directory authentication.

front: What port does Microsoft SQL Server operate on by default?
back: TCP port 1433. Relational database client query protocol utilized for structured enterprise data operations.

front: What ports and transport protocols are used by Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) for VoIP signaling in cleartext vs encrypted mode?
back: Port 5060 (TCP/UDP) for cleartext SIP VoIP signaling; Port 5061 (TCP) for SIP over TLS (encrypted multimedia signaling).

front: What are the core functions, data formats, and technologies of Layer 6 (Presentation) in the OSI model?
back: PDU: Data. Handles character encoding/translation (ASCII, Unicode), data compression/formatting (JPEG, GIF, MPEG), and cryptographic TLS/SSL encryption and decryption processes.

front: What are the core functions and representative protocols of Layer 5 (Session) in the OSI model?
back: PDU: Data. Establishes, controls, checkpoints, and terminates dialogues and communication sessions between local and remote applications. Protocols: RPC, NetBIOS, SQL Sockets, NFS, Named Pipes.

front: What are the two distinct sublayers of Layer 2 (Data Link) and their respective functions?
back:
1. LLC (Logical Link Control, IEEE 802.2): Interacts with Layer 3 Network layer, handles flow control, error checking, and frame multiplexing.
2. MAC (Media Access Control): Controls hardware physical addressing (48-bit MAC) and media access rules (CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA).

front: Detail the byte/packet-level exchange and architectural significance of the TCP three-way handshake.
back: Sequence: SYN (client ISN) -> SYN-ACK (server ISN, ACK client ISN+1) -> ACK (client ACK server ISN+1). Establishes Transmission Control Blocks (TCBs), synchronizes initial sequence numbers, and negotiates Maximum Segment Size (MSS) and window scale.

front: What is the four-step sequence for graceful TCP connection teardown and why is it structured this way?
back: Sequence: FIN -> ACK (from receiver), then FIN -> ACK (from sender). Coordinates full-duplex session termination, ensuring both communication endpoints independently flush and close their respective transmission buffers.

front: What is Direct Attach Copper (DAC) cabling and where is it typically deployed?
back: Factory-integrated twinaxial copper cable assembly with fixed SFP+ or QSFP transceivers (1 to 7 meters). Delivers high-speed (up to 100 Gbps), ultra-low latency, and low cost for intra-rack top-of-rack switch-to-server interconnects.

front: Compare Plenum-rated (CMP) vs Riser-rated (CMR) cabling in fire rating and installation criteria.
back:
Plenum (CMP): Jacketed in low-smoke, low-flame Fluorinated Ethylene Polymer (FEP). Mandated by fire safety codes in drop ceilings and raised floors acting as environmental air return ducts.
Riser (CMR): Flame-retardant PVC engineered to prevent vertical fire spread through floor penetrations; strictly forbidden in plenum air handling spaces.

front: Differentiate the supported port speeds and physical density profiles of SFP, SFP+, QSFP+, and QSFP28 transceivers.
back:
SFP: Up to 1 Gbps (standard modular Gigabit).
SFP+: Up to 10 Gbps (shares standard SFP footprint).
QSFP / QSFP+: 40 Gbps (bundles 4 x 10 Gbps lanes for datacenter uplinks).
QSFP28: 100 Gbps (bundles 4 x 25 Gbps lanes for modern spine-and-leaf switches).

front: Compare legacy Wi-Fi standards 802.11b, 802.11a, and 802.11g in frequency, maximum theoretical speed, and modulation.
back:
802.11b: 2.4 GHz, 11 Mbps, DSSS / CCK, 20 MHz channel.
802.11a: 5 GHz, 54 Mbps, OFDM, 20 MHz channel.
802.11g: 2.4 GHz, 54 Mbps, OFDM, 20 MHz channel.

front: Compare 802.11n (Wi-Fi 4) and 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5) in frequency bands, modulation, and maximum theoretical speeds.
back:
Wi-Fi 4 (802.11n): 2.4 & 5 GHz, up to 600 Mbps, MIMO (up to 4 spatial streams), 64-QAM, 20/40 MHz channels.
Wi-Fi 5 (802.11ac): 5 GHz only, up to 6.93 Gbps, Downlink MU-MIMO, 256-QAM, channel widths up to 80/160 MHz.

front: What are the non-overlapping channels in the 2.4 GHz spectrum in North America (FCC) and why does channel overlap cause issues?
back: Channels 1, 6, and 11 (each spaced 25 MHz apart with 20 MHz channel widths). Deploying adjacent APs on overlapping channels (e.g. 2, 3, 4, 5) creates adjacent-channel interference (ACI), collisions, and packet retries.

front: What architectural vulnerability affects WPA2-Personal (PSK) and how does WPA3-Personal resolve it?
back:
WPA2-Personal uses a single PSK vulnerable to offline dictionary brute-force attacks via captured 4-way EAPOL handshakes.
WPA3-Personal replaces PSK with Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE / Dragonfly handshake), providing forward secrecy and rendering captured handshakes useless for offline cracking.

front: Explain the three functional entities of 802.1X Network Access Control and its security benefits over WPA-Personal.
back:
Entities: Supplicant (client software), Authenticator (switch/AP permitting only EAPoL traffic until authed), Authentication Server (RADIUS/TACACS+).
Benefits: Eliminates shared pre-shared keys, authenticates individual user directory accounts, and generates dynamic per-user/per-session encryption keys.

front: Differentiate EAP-TLS, PEAP, and EAP-TTLS authentication mechanisms in certificate requirements.
back:
EAP-TLS: Requires mutual authentication where BOTH the server and client validate each other via X.509 digital certificates (highest security).
PEAP: Only the server presents an X.509 certificate to establish an encrypted TLS tunnel; client authenticates via username/password (MS-CHAPv2).
EAP-TTLS: Server presents a certificate tunnel; supports multiple inner client authentication methods.

front: What is the IPv4 Multicast address range (Class D) and what protocols manage multicast routing?
back: 224.0.0.0/4 (224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255, RFC 5771). Delivers one-to-many communications without broadcasting; routed by multicast protocols such as PIM (Protocol Independent Multicast) and managed locally via IGMP.

front: Explain how IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) and EUI-64 generate a 128-bit address.
back:
SLAAC: Host receives a 64-bit network prefix via ICMPv6 Router Advertisements (RA) from local routers.
EUI-64: Host generates its 64-bit Interface ID by splitting its 48-bit MAC address in half, inserting 16-bit 0xFFFE in the middle, and inverting the 7th bit (Universal/Local bit). (e.g. 00:11:22:33:44:55 -> 0211:22ff:fe33:4455).

front: What is the purpose of running `ping -f -l 1472 <IP>` on Windows?
back: Discovers Path MTU without fragmentation. `-f` sets the DF (Don't Fragment) bit; `-l 1472` specifies 1472 bytes of ICMP payload. Adding 20 bytes IP header + 8 bytes ICMP header = exactly 1500 bytes (standard Ethernet MTU).

front: Explain the syntax and purpose of Windows `tracert -d` and Linux `traceroute -n -T`.
back:
Windows `tracert -d`: Skips reverse DNS lookup for each hop, accelerating path tracing.
Linux `traceroute -n -T`: `-n` skips DNS resolution, and `-T` sends TCP SYN packets to port 80/443 instead of UDP, successfully traversing firewalls that drop UDP probes.

front: What specific outputs are provided by `netstat -ano` versus `netstat -r`?
back:
`netstat -ano`: Displays all active connections and listening ports numerically (-n) alongside their Process Identifiers (PID, -o).
`netstat -r`: Displays the host operating system's local Layer 3 IPv4/IPv6 routing table.

front: What does the `+trace` option do in the BIND `dig` utility?
back: Performs iterative, hierarchical DNS resolution starting from the 13 Root DNS servers (root hints), following delegation down to TLD (.com) servers, and finally querying authoritative nameservers, displaying full response times and delegation flags.

front: In `tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -s 0 port 80 -w capture.pcap`, what do the `-nn` and `-s 0` flags accomplish?
back:
`-nn`: Prevents protocol and port name resolution (keeps IP addresses and ports numeric to avoid DNS delays).
`-s 0`: Sets snaplen to 0 (captures the entire packet payload without truncation for Wireshark inspection).

front: What is `iperf3` used for and what does `iperf3 -c <IP> -u -b 100M` measure?
back:
Measures throughput and network performance between client and server endpoints.
`-c <IP>`: Client mode targeting server.
`-u`: Tests UDP datagrams instead of TCP.
`-b 100M`: Sets target bandwidth to 100 Mbps, measuring UDP jitter, packet loss, and out-of-order delivery.

front: Differentiate MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) and MTTR (Mean Time to Repair).
back:
MTBF: Quantifies equipment reliability by calculating the average operating time between unexpected hardware breakdowns.
MTTR: Measures maintainability and service recovery speed by calculating the average time required to diagnose, repair, and restore a failed system to production.

front: Differentiate Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO) in disaster recovery.
back:
RTO (Recovery Time Objective): Maximum acceptable duration of service downtime before operational harm occurs (Time limit to restore).
RPO (Recovery Point Objective): Maximum acceptable threshold of data loss measured in time backwards from disruption (Data age acceptable to lose).

front: Compare SNMPv1/v2c security with SNMPv3 User-Based Security Model (USM).
back:
SNMPv1/v2c: Uses clear-text 'community strings' (public/private) for authorization with zero payload encryption or integrity checks.
SNMPv3: Introduces USM supporting authPriv mode, providing HMAC-MD5/SHA message integrity/authentication and CBC-DES/AES packet encryption.

front: When should an engineer employ Bottom-Up, Top-Down, or Divide-and-Conquer troubleshooting?
back:
Bottom-Up (L1->L7): Suspected physical cabling, transceiver, or switchport link light issues.
Top-Down (L7->L1): Connectivity is intact but specific applications, DNS lookups, or HTTP APIs fail.
Divide-and-Conquer (L3 first): Starts with gateway ping; success immediately rules out L1/L2 and ARP, isolating faults to L4-L7.

front: What is the golden rule when creating a Variable Length Subnet Masking (VLSM) addressing plan?
back: Subnets must ALWAYS be allocated starting from the LARGEST host requirement down to the SMALLEST host requirement. Violating this rule causes overlapping boundaries and fragmented, unusable IP address blocks.

front: Explain the 'Longest Prefix Match' rule in Layer 3 IP routing.
back: A router always forwards packets matching the route with the most specific (highest) prefix length (e.g., /24 beats /16 and /8), regardless of whether another route has a lower Administrative Distance or better metric.

front: Order these routing sources by Administrative Distance from most preferred (lowest AD) to least: Static, OSPF, eBGP, RIP, Connected, EIGRP (internal).
back:
1. Connected (0)
2. Static (1)
3. External BGP / eBGP (20)
4. Internal EIGRP (90)
5. OSPF (110)
6. RIP (120)

front: What are the 4 sub-fields within a 32-bit (4-byte) IEEE 802.1Q VLAN tag?
back:
1. TPID (16 bits): Tag Protocol ID, set to 0x8100.
2. PCP (3 bits): Priority Code Point, marks Class of Service (CoS) for L2 QoS.
3. DEI (1 bit): Drop Eligible Indicator, marks frames drop-eligible during congestion.
4. VID (12 bits): VLAN ID, supporting up to 4,096 VLANs (1-4094 usable).

front: How does an 802.1Q Double-Tagging Attack work and how is it mitigated?
back:
Attack: Attacker sends frame with two 802.1Q tags where the outer tag matches the trunk's Native VLAN. The first switch strips the outer tag and sends the frame untagged. The second switch reads the inner tag and forwards it into a restricted target VLAN, bypassing firewalls.
Mitigation: Change Native VLAN from default 1 to an unused VLAN ID and force tagging on native traffic (vlan dot1q tag native).

front: How is the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) Root Bridge elected?
back: Switches exchange BPDUs containing their Bridge ID (BID). The BID consists of Bridge Priority (default 32,768 in steps of 4,096) + base MAC address. The switch with the lowest numerical BID is elected Root Bridge.

front: Compare Classic STP (802.1D) vs Rapid STP (802.1w) in convergence time and transition mechanisms.
back:
Classic STP (802.1D): 30-50 seconds convergence; relies on static timers (20s Max Age, 15s Forward Delay across Blocking, Listening, Learning, Forwarding).
Rapid STP (802.1w): Millisecond convergence; replaces static timers with proactive Proposal-Agreement handshakes across Discarding, Learning, and Forwarding states.

front: What happens if two switch interfaces connected via an Ethernet trunk are both configured in LACP Passive mode?
back: The link will FAIL to aggregate into a Port-Channel. In Passive mode, a port responds to LACP packets but never initiates negotiation. At least one end must be configured in Active mode for LACP trunking to establish.

front: Explain the cabling topology and traffic advantages of a Spine-and-Leaf (Clos) datacenter architecture.
back:
Topology: Every Leaf switch connects to every Spine switch in a full mesh. Leaf switches never connect to leaf switches, and spine switches never connect to spine switches.
Advantages: Optimized for East-West server-to-server traffic; provides deterministic, predictable single-hop latency between any two servers using Layer 3 ECMP load balancing.

front: What transport protocol, destination port, and identifier does VXLAN utilize?
back: Transport: UDP destination port 4789. Uses a 24-bit VXLAN Network Identifier (VNI) supporting over 16 million logical segments (compared to 4,096 in 802.1Q). Terminated by VXLAN Tunnel Endpoints (VTEPs) over Layer 3 IP underlays.

front: Differentiate the Management, Control, and Data planes in Software-Defined Networking (SDN).
back:
Management Plane: Admin interfaces (SSH, HTTPS, API, SNMP).
Control Plane: Routing logic, topology calculation, and path tables (OSPF, BGP, STP); centralized in the SDN controller.
Data Plane: High-speed hardware packet forwarding and frame switching via ASICs.
Communication uses Southbound APIs (OpenFlow, NETCONF, RESTCONF).

front: What is SD-WAN and what does Zero-Touch Provisioning (ZTP) accomplish?
back:
SD-WAN: Application-aware software overlay aggregating hybrid WAN links (MPLS, broadband, 5G) into an encrypted fabric with dynamic traffic steering.
ZTP (Zero-Touch Provisioning): Allows newly connected edge branch appliances to automatically boot, fetch configurations, download policies, and register certificates with zero manual on-site engineer configuration.

front: What are the three core operational pillars of Zero-Trust Architecture (NIST SP 800-207)?
back:
1. Microsegmentation (isolating workloads into granular security zones to prevent lateral movement).
2. Continuous Adaptive Verification (session-long assessment of device health, user context, and anomalies).
3. Least-Privilege Enforcement (strictly limiting access to the minimum permissions required).

front: Map these 4 Layer 2 attacks to their primary switch mitigation: MAC Flooding, Rogue DHCP, ARP Poisoning, STP Hijacking.
back:
1. MAC Flooding (CAM exhaustion) -> Port Security (mac-address sticky, errdisable).
2. Rogue DHCP / Starvation -> DHCP Snooping (trusted vs untrusted ports).
3. ARP Poisoning (MitM) -> Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI, checks DHCP snooping DB).
4. STP Hijacking -> BPDU Guard (shuts down PortFast ports receiving BPDUs) and Root Guard.

front: Compare HSRP, VRRP, and GLBP in standard status, preemption defaults, and load-balancing capabilities.
back:
HSRP: Cisco proprietary; Active/Standby; preemption disabled by default; virtual MAC 0000.0c07.acXX.
VRRP: IETF open standard (RFC 5798); Master/Backup; preemption ENABLED by default; virtual MAC 00-00-5E-00-01-XX.
GLBP: Cisco proprietary; Active Virtual Gateway (AVG) assigns up to 4 Active Virtual Forwarders (AVFs), providing true active-active load balancing.

front: Compare Cold Site, Warm Site, and Hot Site (Active-Active) in readiness, RTO, and RPO.
back:
Cold Site: Space/power/cooling only, no hardware, days-to-weeks RTO, high data loss RPO, lowest cost.
Warm Site: Hardware pre-racked, periodic backups (no live mirror), hours-to-days RTO and RPO, moderate cost.
Hot Site (Active-Active): Redundant live clusters, synchronous replication, near-zero instantaneous RTO and zero transactional data loss RPO, highest cost.
